title: Gender & articles
body: Italian nouns have a grammatical gender. Il is common before masculine nouns, lo before z or s + consonant, and l’ before a vowel. La is feminine; it becomes l’ before a vowel. Plurals are i, gli, and le. Indefinite articles are un, uno, una, and un’.

title: Making plurals
body: Many nouns change -o to -i, -a to -e, and -e to -i. Some are irregular: l’uovo → le uova. Words with a final written accent often stay unchanged: la città → le città.

title: Subject pronouns
body: Io, tu, lui/lei, noi, voi, loro mean I, you, he/she, we, you plural, they. Italian often leaves the pronoun out because the verb ending already identifies the subject. Lei is also formal singular you.

title: Essere & avere
body: Essere means to be: sono, sei, è, siamo, siete, sono. Avere means to have: ho, hai, ha, abbiamo, avete, hanno. Italian uses avere for age and several feelings.

body: Remove -are and add -o, -i, -a, -iamo, -ate, -ano. Parlare becomes parlo, parli, parla, parliamo, parlate, parlano. Keep spelling changes in mind: pagare → paghi.

title: Common irregular verbs
body: Frequent verbs often have irregular present forms. Andare: vado, vai, va, andiamo, andate, vanno. Fare: faccio, fai, fa, facciamo, fate, fanno. Learn their forms with short useful sentences.

title: Adjective agreement
body: Adjectives agree with their noun in gender and number. Many have four endings: -o, -a, -i, -e. Adjectives ending in -e usually have plural -i for both genders.

title: Everyday prepositions
body: A commonly marks cities and destinations; in marks countries and many places. Di expresses origin or possession. Da can mark a starting point or a person’s place. Su means on, per often means for.

title: Articulated prepositions
body: Di, a, da, in, and su can combine with definite articles. Di + il = del; a + il = al; da + il = dal; in + il = nel; su + il = sul. With la: della, alla, dalla, nella, sulla.

examples.native: I am going to the market.

title: Questions & negation
body: Many yes/no questions use the same word order as statements, with questioning intonation. Put non directly before the verb to make a negative. Question words include chi, dove, quando, come, and perché.

title: Passato prossimo
body: Build this past tense with present avere or essere plus a past participle. Regular endings: -are → -ato, -ere → -uto, -ire → -ito, with many irregulars. With essere, the participle agrees with the subject.

title: Possessives
body: Possessives agree with the thing possessed: il mio libro, la mia casa, i miei libri, le mie case. Singular unmodified family nouns usually omit the article: mia madre, mio padre. Loro keeps the article.
